title: Early warning before an excursion, plus the what-if lab
description: Replay starts at 07:55 (glucose 94 mg/dL, excursion risk about 22%, no alert). Step forward to see the alert fire at 08:55, right after the logged 140 g breakfast, 85 min before glucose first exceeds 180 mg/dL (10:20). What-ifs are recorded at 07:55 and 08:55 (2 min after the breakfast: larger hypothetical meals then fall outside training support because the model counts carbs over the last 30 min).

primary.label: vs a zero-carb meal at the same time (isolates the carb content)

secondary.label: vs no meal (also includes the model's learned meal-timing expectation)

notes: Meals under 30 g are unreliable in this model: few training meals are that small and the audited small-meal differences are unstable.
Logging any meal now (even zero-carb) shifts the risk by -14 points on its own: a learned meal-timing association, not physiology. That is why the no-meal comparison differs.

joint_support.caveat: Training-support check: it flags meal inputs with no comparable example in the training data. It is not evidence that the forecast is wrong, and inputs inside the training range do not make a forecast accurate.

outside_tested_reasons: meal size outside the tested 20-120 g
twin_curve.caveat: Research estimate, not the served forecast. Fitted on synthetic training patients, selected on validation patients and tested once on held-out synthetic patients against simulator ground truth; the simulator's near-linear meal response favours it. The walk effect is cohort level (the twin has no personal activity parameter) and reflects the simulator's built-in exercise model. Not evidence about real patients; not advice.

result.disclaimer: Simulated what-if scenario. The hypothetical meal was never added to the patient record. Differences are learned associations of the forecasting models, not causal physiological effects. Not medical advice and not a treatment recommendation.

twin_curve.caveat: Research estimate, not the served forecast. primary.label: vs a zero-carb meal at the same time (isolates the carb content)

notes: Logging any meal now (even zero-carb) shifts the +60-min forecast by -15.1 mg/dL and the risk by -13 points on its own: a learned meal-timing association, not physiology. That is why the no-meal comparison differs.

joint_support.caveat: Training-support check: it flags meal inputs with no comparable example in the training data. It is not evidence that the forecast is wrong, and inputs inside the training range do not make a forecast accurate.

twin_curve.caveat: Research estimate, not the served forecast. Fitted on synthetic training patients, selected on validation patients and tested once on held-out synthetic patients against simulator ground truth; the simulator's near-linear meal response favours it. The walk effect is cohort level (the twin has no personal activity parameter) and reflects the simulator's built-in exercise model. Not evidence about real patients; not advice.

result.disclaimer: Simulated what-if scenario. The hypothetical meal was never added to the patient record. Differences are learned associations of the forecasting models, not causal physiological effects. Not medical advice and not a treatment recommendation.

primary.label: vs a zero-carb meal at the same time (isolates the carb content)

secondary.label: vs no meal (also includes the model's learned meal-timing expectation)

notes: Starting risk is already above 95%, so the risk change is not informative.
Logging any meal now (even zero-carb) shifts the +60-min forecast by -2.8 mg/dL on its own: a learned meal-timing association, not physiology. That is why the no-meal comparison differs.

joint_support.caveat: Training-support check: it flags meal inputs with no comparable example in the training data. It is not evidence that the forecast is wrong, and inputs inside the training range do not make a forecast accurate.

twin_curve.caveat: Research estimate, not the served forecast. Fitted on synthetic training patients, selected on validation patients and tested once on held-out synthetic patients against simulator ground truth; the simulator's near-linear meal response favours it. The walk effect is cohort level (the twin has no personal activity parameter) and reflects the simulator's built-in exercise model. Not evidence about real patients; not advice.

result.disclaimer: Simulated what-if scenario. The hypothetical meal was never added to the patient record. Differences are learned associations of the forecasting models, not causal physiological effects. Not medical advice and not a treatment recommendation.

primary.label: vs a zero-carb meal at the same time (isolates the carb content)

joint_support.caveat: Training-support check: it flags meal inputs with no comparable example in the training data. It is not evidence that the forecast is wrong, and inputs inside the training range do not make a forecast accurate.

twin_curve.caveat: Research estimate, not the served forecast. Fitted on synthetic training patients, selected on validation patients and tested once on held-out synthetic patients against simulator ground truth; the simulator's near-linear meal response favours it. The walk effect is cohort level (the twin has no personal activity parameter) and reflects the simulator's built-in exercise model. Not evidence about real patients; not advice.

result.disclaimer: Simulated what-if scenario. The hypothetical meal was never added to the patient record. Differences are learned associations of the forecasting models, not causal physiological effects. Not medical advice and not a treatment recommendation.

twin_curve.caveat: Research estimate, not the served forecast. result.disclaimer: Simulated what-if scenario. The hypothetical meal was never added to the patient record. Differences are learned associations of the forecasting models, not causal physiological effects. Not medical advice and not a treatment recommendation.
